newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister wants car groups to cooperate.
newsitem.headline: French minister wants car groups to cooperate.

text.p: French Industry Minister Franck Borotra told the Les Echos newspaper in an interview that he wanted the country's car makers to cooperate more in order to cut their costs and become more competitive.

He said that the government would be unwilling to accept a proposal made by the car groups, planning to rejuvenate their workforce by a five-year programme of early retirements, if there was not also an industrial plan.
Borotra said he had appointed Bernard Cabaret, a retired car industry executive, to study the matter and report back in the second half of January.
Borotra declined to confirm reports that the car makers sought to shed 40,000 jobs in exchange for hiring 14,000 youngsters, nor the estimated cost of 30 billion francs.
"At this stage in the discussions, I can say that the demands have not been finalised but that there would have an very important human and financial cost," Borotra said.
He said the car makers' plans, as they lay on the table, were not in line with government policy. But he wanted a study of the industry's situation to find a common solution.
"No more social plans (lay-offs) without an industrial project," he said.
Borotra said that with the changing competitive situation, particularly the opening up of the European car market to Japanese exports, French companies needed to cut their costs.
"The reduction of costs is necessarily going to be the effect of economies of scale and therefore of case-by-case cooperation," he said.

"They (the two car groups) make an engine and a gearbox (together). We have to go further and look what they can do as well, whether it is in cross part supply, joint production of low volume vehicles to sharing investment costs in emerging markets, or closer structures," Borotra said.

"PSA Peugeot Citroen and Renault have developed a policy of cooperation with each other. They have also done it with other leading companies in the world. That's one of the elements of the industry's answer (to the new competitive environment)," Borotra said.

Satirical weekly Le Canard Enchainee said last week that the chairmen of the two companies had written to Prime Minister Alain Juppe with a proposal to reduce the average age of their workforce. In this week's issue, the weekly said that the car makers wanted to speed up the plan and execute it over six years instead of 10.
